Thread to discuss the Lean formalization of the RH bounds improvements that Anthropic made today - https://www.anthropic.com/research/riemann-zeta and the lean repo https://github.com/anthropics/zeta-23-lean.

I see a comparitor setup (but no github CI run?) and comments and file layout were kept. According to Claude's analysis - 100k loc, 42 max_heartbeats increases, no axioms or sorries.
Again, lean formalization released at the time of the paper announcement.

As a lay-person, how significant is this to real mathematicians? My understanding is that a real proof probably wouldn't build off of a lower bound improvement. And that moving the lower bound to 100% is the hard part. Am I right in thinking this just tells us we could be a little more confident that RH is really true?

Duplicate thread of #general > Anthropic's formalization of zeta

Alex Sweeney said:

As a lay-person, how significant is this to real mathematicians? My understanding is that a real proof probably wouldn't build off of a lower bound improvement. And that moving the lower bound to 100% is the hard part. Am I right in thinking this just tells us we could be a little more confident that RH is really true?

Even moving the lower bound to 100%, in the sense of this result, wouldn't actually prove RH. If only one zero is off the line, then the fraction would still be 100%.
Otoh, I think that we can now tongue-in-cheek say that RH is more than 50% true (-;
Time to rehash the old joke: perhaps Anthropic can approach Clay and ask for two thirds of the $1M.
Has anyone reviewed the lean code? I guess it's using mathlib definitions, so the main statement may be easy to verify (?)

Yup, the Challenge.lean file makes this very easy. You need to read < 30 lines of code to reduce everything to Mathlib concepts. I checked it, and I'm happy to vouch for correctness.

(Edit: I should add that I didn't run comparator myself. I've only read the code.)

And https://github.com/anthropics/zeta-23-lean/blob/main/comparator/Challenge.lean imports https://github.com/anthropics/zeta-23-lean/blob/main/comparator/ChallengeDeps.lean so you have to read all of that too.

Well, for Theorem A in Challenge.lean, you only need the first < 30% of ChallengeDeps.lean.
Anyways, it's all very short and readable. 5 mins should suffice for anyone who trusts mathlib, and wants to understand the statements.

I'm not sure I agree with this; to me, it seems like there are rather a lot of junk value corner cases that require careful thinking

@Eric Wieser Hmmm, can you say more? All those junk value edges are part of Mathlib right? And the only one that comes to mind to me right now is the pole of ζ\zetaζ, whose junk value was computed to be non-zero by David Loeffler some time ago.
3 messages were moved from this topic to #AI authored projects > junk values and trusting statements by Johan Commelin.

I would like to just express an appreciation that big AI labs care about formal math, and provide a well-checkable Lean proof. When I first heard of this in mainstream news, my first reaction was "can I trust it?". I don't think it can get much better for AI math results, and happy to see this becoming the standard.

@Johan Commelin, things like

/-- N(T₁,T₂): the number of nontrivial zeros with T₁ < Im ρ ≤ T₂, counted WITH multiplicity
(`∑ᶠ` is Mathlib's finite sum; that the window contains finitely many zeros is proved on the
solution side, not assumed). -/
def Ncount (T₁ T₂ : ℝ) : ℕ := ∑ᶠ ρ ∈ zerosIn T₁ T₂, zeroMult ρ

/-- N_d(T₁,T₂): the number of nontrivial zeros with T₁ < Im ρ ≤ T₂, each distinct zero counted
once. -/
def Ndist (T₁ T₂ : ℝ) : ℕ := (zerosIn T₁ T₂).ncard

make me worry; now I need to check that zerosIn is proved finite anywhere that uses these definitions, or think about whether it still does the right thing when it is not finite. There are a large number of ncards in this formalization.

Perhaps it is obvious that this set is finite, but as the reader I Ideally shouldn't have to be coming up with proofs to justify that the statement is correct when the whole point of presenting a solution in Lean is to avoid the reader having to do any proofs.
It's a standard mathematical fact that a nonzero meromorphic function will only have finitely many zeros on a compact subset of the plane.

Kevin Buzzard said:

It's a standard mathematical fact

But is it formally proved in Lean?
I don't know, but isn't the question "could this be a junk value"? I'm just saying the answer is "undergraduate complex analysis says no"
@Eric Wieser Fair enough. I agree that ideally the fact Kevin mentions would be used, and then a finset is used instead of ncard or other junk values.

To be clear, this isn't really a criticism of Anthropic's formalization; rather than this demonstrates a simple form of a much larger failure mode, and it seems like something that falls on Mathlib to try and steer away from.

In particular, Anthropic's comment:

that the window contains finitely many zeros is proved on the solution side, not assumed

Is sort of saying "the comparator Challenge.lean mechanism isn't enough to ensure trustworthiness, you have to look at (or know some of) the proof to check the junk values don't happen"

Maybe there should be not just private and public scopes, but also an AI scope where the functions that take junk values in the private/public scope actually take the proof obligations at AI scope and AIs are only allowed to use AI scope.

Eric Wieser said:

In particular, Anthropic's comment:

that the window contains finitely many zeros is proved on the solution side, not assumed

Is sort of saying "the comparator Challenge.lean mechanism isn't enough to ensure trustworthiness, you have to look at (or know some of) the proof to check the junk values don't happen"

I agree with this. The challenge statements only capture the intended theorem "modulo undergraduate knowledge." The full literal theorem statement for e.g. two_thirds_on_critical_line_cumulative should directly correspond to the statement "these windows all have a positive finite number of zeroes, whose proportion on the critical line has liminf at least 2/3."

But perhaps it's naive to complain about this, considering informally stated results generally are equivalence classes of "mod undergrad equivalent" assertions rather than uniquely reducible to formalism.

Eric Wieser said:

In particular, Anthropic's comment:

that the window contains finitely many zeros is proved on the solution side, not assumed

Is sort of saying "the comparator Challenge.lean mechanism isn't enough to ensure trustworthiness, you have to look at (or know some of) the proof to check the junk values don't happen"

Or use Set.encard in the statement instead, which doesn't suffer from the junk value problem.

Setting aside this specific example, I think that the concern isn't so much that undergraduate math is assumed, but that objects aren't always defined exactly how I expect them to be defined. If I read a piece of Lean code and see a reference to the Riemann zeta function, then my natural tendency is to assume that it means what people usually mean by the Riemann zeta function, not something that is almost the same as the Riemann zeta function except that it is defined to be something funny at the pole. This increases my cognitive load when trying to verify that the formal theorem statement says what it appears to say. (The Mind-Reading Problem!)

An interesting challenge might be to craft a valid proof of a valid theorem (not exploiting any bugs in Lean), which depends only on Mathlib, but where 99% of humans reading the theorem think that it says something (ideally something false) other than what it really says, and don't suspect that anything might be fishy. Is AI better than humans at this game?
precisely. It's not impossible to formalize functions in mathlib (a "wrapper" as one may say) that keep track of all the junk values, is it?

@Timothy Chow I think @Riccardo Brasca has an example of this in number theory (something cyclotomic fields) that came up in FLT-regular. I don't remember the details, but I think it has to do with a p = 2 case?
Hmm, are you thinking to IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.discr_prime_pow? The docstring says everything, but basically it's a theorem that holds in an edge case because of a junk value.
You can compare wikipedia, where n > 2 is assumed.
How about "there exists a real number x such that 1/x=0"? Lean thinks this is true and humans think it's false and the proof in lean is easy

"There exists a real number x such that 1/x = 0" is nice but obviously fishy. I'm envisaging a Challenge.lean file where almost everyone reads it and says, "Yes, that's a correct formalization of X" when in fact it's not.

For example, if we had the junk value zeta(1) = 0 then "There is a zero that is not a negative even number and does not have real part 1/2" would be a theorem and would look a lot like the negation of the Riemann hypothesis. This particular example doesn't work, but surely(?) someone, perhaps with AI assistance, can come up with an example that does work.

So the challenge is to come up with a real-world theorem which is true/has an informal proof, and a subtle misformalization of the statement of that theorem such that the misformalized theorem is also true, but the misformalized proof is maybe much less complex than the proof of the real theorem would be so that it's not just a simple nonhandling of an edge case?

Claude Opus 5's proof.

Here's a "proof" that the solution to the Hadwiger-Nelson problem is at least 4 based on a misconception I once had:

Opus 5

import Mathlib

namespace HadwigerNelson

/-- The plane: a point is given by its two real coordinates. -/
abbrev Plane := Fin 2 → ℝ

/-- A colouring of the plane is *proper* if no two points at distance `1` receive the
same colour. -/
def Proper {n : ℕ} (c : Plane → Fin n) : Prop :=
  ∀ p q : Plane, dist p q = 1 → c p ≠ c q

/-- **The chromatic number of the plane is at least `4`**: no colouring of the plane with
three colours avoids giving two points at distance `1` the same colour. -/
theorem three_colours_not_enough : ¬ ∃ c : Plane → Fin 3, Proper c := by
  rintro ⟨c, hc⟩
  obtain ⟨h₁, h₂, h₃, h₄, h₅, h₆⟩ :
      c ![0, 0] ≠ c ![1, 0] ∧ c ![0, 0] ≠ c ![0, 1] ∧ c ![0, 0] ≠ c ![1, 1] ∧
        c ![1, 0] ≠ c ![0, 1] ∧ c ![1, 0] ≠ c ![1, 1] ∧ c ![0, 1] ≠ c ![1, 1] := by
    refine ⟨hc _ _ ?_, hc _ _ ?_, hc _ _ ?_, hc _ _ ?_, hc _ _ ?_, hc _ _ ?_⟩ <;>
      norm_num [dist_pi_eq_iff, Fin.exists_fin_two, Fin.forall_fin_two, Real.dist_eq]
  simp only [ne_eq, Fin.ext_iff] at h₁ h₂ h₃ h₄ h₅ h₆
  have b₀ := (c ![(0:ℝ), 0]).isLt
  have b₁ := (c ![(1:ℝ), 0]).isLt
  have b₂ := (c ![(0:ℝ), 1]).isLt
  have b₃ := (c ![(1:ℝ), 1]).isLt
  omega

end HadwigerNelson
